ratings.rationale: Unauthenticated fabricated emissions constitute spoofing and create false targets. Practical ADS-B attack demonstrations support E2, although satellite-specific consequences are less established. Cross-checking may expose fabricated targets independently of HDOP; W2 and W3 concern single-satellite timing bias, not this mechanism.
ratings.issue: Asset scope omits A1.3 and A1.4, which receive and extract the fabricated emissions.

ratings.rationale: Rebroadcasting genuine messages creates stale or geographically misleading observations, combining source spoofing with replay tampering. Practical ADS-B replay evidence supports the mechanism, but the cited evidence does not establish its effectiveness against satellite multilateration. Cross-checking and temporal consistency may expose discrepancies.
ratings.issue: Replay is distinct from fabrication, but freshness and duplicate-message handling are unspecified; the claimed displaced-position consequence is conditional.

ratings.rationale: A genuine aircraft transmitting an incorrect position tampers with its self-reported data while retaining genuine reception geometry. Independent localisation can identify the discrepancy, making a missed cross-check essential to deception. Evidence for the exact satellite architecture is insufficient; cited source details and applicability remain uncertain.
ratings.issue: The masking chain is not specified. A wrong broadcast position alone does not defeat independent localisation or establish a nominal integrity verdict.

ratings.rationale: In-band interference degrades reception and prevents valid measurement extraction, constituting denial rather than spoofing. Practical terrestrial ADS-B interference evidence supports the mechanism, but satellite-specific evidence is weaker. RF monitoring or reception-quality checks can identify interference at L1 independently of timing-pass conditions.
ratings.issue: The stated mechanism supports denial, but affected geographic coverage and constellation-wide consequences are not quantified.

missing_threats.title: GNSS reception or timing disruption
missing_threats.why: GNSS disruption can corrupt onboard timing and positioning dependencies independently of fabricated ADS-B content.

missing_threats.title: Payload measurement extraction compromise
missing_threats.why: Compromised extraction firmware could alter TOA, FOA or AOA while preserving apparently valid reports.

missing_threats.title: Onboard oscillator instability
missing_threats.why: Clock drift or disciplining failure can create systematic measurement errors without deliberate RF interference.

missing_threats.title: Antenna beam manipulation or degradation
missing_threats.why: Antenna faults or manipulation can corrupt AOA measurements or reduce reception independently of jamming.

rubric_ambiguities: W2 and W3 specify detection of single-satellite timing bias, not detection of fabricated, replayed or falsified ADS-B messages.
Di is defined by detection predicates, but no explicit predicates or detection coverage are supplied for these four threats.
Evidence levels do not distinguish practical terrestrial demonstrations from satellite-specific demonstrations except through analogue_only.
The affected-user scale does not define how multiple aircraft affected within one satellite footprint should be counted.
A false aircraft position can produce displacement or deception depending on whether the fabricated target is genuine or nonexistent.
batch_comments.overall: All four mechanisms are distinct and defensively relevant. Fabrication, replay, falsified self-reported position and RF denial should not be collapsed into one threat. The largest modelling weakness is transferring terrestrial ADS-B attack evidence directly to LEO multilateration without establishing the corresponding satellite-system consequences. Detection ratings also require threat-specific predicates rather than automatically inheriting the timing assumptions.
